    1                                            I.       INTRODUCTION

    2           Plaintiff Courtney Van Cott seeks preliminary approval of a proposed class action settlement that

    3   provides Settlement Class Members the full value of the late-fee reimbursements sought in this lawsuit.

    4   Balanced against the cost, delay, and risks of further litigation, the relief provided by the settlement is fair,

    5   reasonable, and adequate within the meaning of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(e) and satisfies all of

    6   the criteria for preliminary settlement approval. Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court: (i)

    7   preliminarily approve the settlement; (ii) certify the proposed Settlement Class and appoint Plaintiff Van

    8   Cott as Settlement Class Representative and Plaintiff’s attorneys as Class Counsel; (iii) approve the

    9   proposed form of the class notice and the notice distribution plan; and (iv) set a fairness hearing.
  10                          II.      FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND

  11            Plaintiff and proposed Settlement Class representative Courtney Van Cott is a former tenant of

  12    Equity Residential in California who was charged and paid a late fee based on Equity’s former “Standard

  13    Late Fee” in September 2023. See Compl., ECF No. 1-1, ¶ 3. Under the Standard Late Fee, in place from

  14    June 2008 through April 2024, Equity charged its California tenants a fee equal to 5% of their monthly

  15    rent, or a minimum of $50, for the late payment of rent. See id. ¶ 1. On April 8, 2024 after trial in the

  16    longstanding related case called Munguia-Brown, et al. v. Equity Residential, et al., Case No. 4:16-cv-

  17    01225-JSW-TSH, this Court held that Equity’s Standard Late Fee is a liquidated damages penalty that is

  18    null and void under California Civil Code section 1671(d) because it is excessive and bears no relation to

  19    any actual damages incurred by Defendants when rent is paid late. See id. ¶ 2 & Ex. A (Munguia-Brown

  20    Court’s Apr. 8, 2024 Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, ECF No. 546 at ¶ 61)), available at 2024

  21    WL 1530571 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 8, 2024). Ms. Van Cott is one of 21,800 proposed Settlement Class

  22    Members here who were charged Equity’s Standard Late Fee, but who are not entitled to monetary relief

  23    in the Munguia-Brown case because they were first charged the Standard Late Fee after the class

  24    definition had closed in that case. See Compl. ¶ 3; Decl. of Linda M. Dardarian in Supp. of Pl’s. Mot. for

  25    Preliminary Approval of Class Action Settlement (“Dardarian Decl.”), filed herewith, ¶ 59.

  26    A.      Munguia-Brown v. Equity Residential
  27            The Munguia-Brown action was filed on September 3, 2014 and removed to this Court on March

  28    11, 2016. See Munguia-Brown, ECF No. 1 & 1-1. Plaintiff’s Counsel here is Class Counsel in that case.

    3   October 23, 2017, the Court granted the plaintiffs’ motion to certify the Standard Late Fee Class, which

    4   encompassed Equity’s California tenants who had been charged the Standard Late Fee on or before

    5   October 23, 2017. 1 See Munguia-Brown, ECF No. 91, 2017 WL 4838822 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 23, 2017). The

    6   Standard Late Fee class was later expanded to encompass monetary relief for all California tenants who

    7   had been charged the Standard Late Fee for the first time between September 3, 2010 through October 28,

    8   2022, based on the then-scheduled trial date, as well as injunctive relief for all current and future tenants.

    9   See Munguia-Brown, ECF No. 315, 2021 WL 4951460 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 25, 2024). Following key rulings
  10    that set the stage for litigating whether Equity had conducted the required reasonable endeavor to set a late
  11    fee based on a fair approximation of its average costs of late rent, as well as Equity’s affirmative defenses
  12    – namely, the scope of actual damages from collecting late rent that Equity could claim to offset
  13    restitution owed to tenants and whether the common law voluntary payment doctrine foreclosed tenants’
  14    recovery; 2 the Court held an eight-day bench trial from June 8 to 21, 2023. See generally ECF No. 1-1,
  15    Ex. A (Munguia-Brown, ECF No. 546).

  16            On April 8, 2024, the Court issued the Munguia-Brown Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law

  17    holding that Equity’s Standard Late Fee violated California Civil Code section 1671(d) and the Unfair

  18    Competition Law, California Business and Professions Code section 17200 et seq., and concluding that the

  19    late fees collected by Equity must be returned to the classes, reduced only by the actual damages caused by

  20    the tenants’ late payment of rent. See ECF No. 546 at 34 ¶¶ 61-62 (2024 WL 1530571). The Court

    1   requested further briefing regarding the final restitution amount, based on plaintiffs’ experts’ data-based

    2   calculations of late fees collected and Equity’s offset for its administrative and interest costs of collecting

    3   late rent, and on proposed injunctive relief. See ECF No. 547. As part of this briefing, plaintiffs’ expert

    4   economist and statistician Andrew Schwarz applied his Court-approved multiple regression analysis to

    5   Equity’s cost data from May 1, 2022 through April 29, 2024 and determined that Equity’s average cost of

    6   collecting late rent for that period totaled $31.98 per late fee. See Munguia-Brown, ECF No. 557-5 at 11

                                   2      A. California Civil Code Section 1671(d).

                                   3      1. To trigger the protections of California Civil Code section 1671(d), Plaintiffs must

                                   7      2. Under California law, liquidated damages are defined as “an amount of compensation to be

                                   8         paid in the event of a breach of contract, the sum of which is fixed and certain by

                                   9         agreement.” Chodos v. W. Publ’g Co., 292 F.3d 992, 1002 (9th Cir. 2002) (quoting Kelly

                                  10         v. McDonald, 98 Cal. App. 121, 125 (1929)). Fees charged for late payments are

                                  11         archetypical liquidated damages provisions. See Garrett v. Coast & S. Fed. Sav. & Loan

                                  12         Ass’n, 9 Cal. 3d 731, 737 (1973) (charges triggered by late payments were governed by

                                  13         California Civil Code section 1671).

                                  14      3. The Standard Late Fee formula, 5% of the outstanding balance with a minimum of $50, is

                                  15         set forth in Equity’s Standard Lease and fixes with certainty an amount of compensation

                                  16         for the breach of a late rent payment. This qualifies as a liquidated damages provision.

                                  17         See Chodos, 292 F.3d at 1002. Likewise, the $50 late fee charged to the Woodland Park

                                  18         Preexisting Lease class was a pre-set amount charged to tenants if they breached their

                                  19         leases by paying late rent.

                                  20      4. California Civil Code section 1671(d) provides that “a provision in a contract liquidating

                                  21         damages for the breach of the contract is void except that the parties to such a contract may

                                  22         agree upon an amount which shall be presumed to be the amount of damage sustained by a

                                  23         breach thereof, when, from the nature of the case, it would be impracticable or extremely

                                  24         difficult to fix the actual damage.”

                                  26         endeavor … to estimate a fair average compensation for any loss that may be sustained” by

                                  27         the breach. See Cal. Civ. Code § 1671(d); Garrett v. Coast & Southern Fed. Sav. & Loan,
